div.head: THEATRE ROYAL.
div.p: THEATRE ROYAL.
Still In The Hands Of The
Auctioneer.
INTERESTING RECOLLECTIONS.

Only a few people attended the sale by public auction of the Theatre Royal, Scotland-road, at the Blue Bell Inn, on .Wednesday afternoon, and despite the persuasiveness and happy prospects foreshadowed by Mr. Herbert Johnson, the auctioneer, it was bought in by a member of the Syndicate at £1,500, after having been declared an open sale at that bid. It is still in the hands of the salesman. • Its history and its possible uses were outlined by Mr. Johnson before he called for bidders. Built in 1883, he said, it had had a prosperous past, and in the hands of a person with initiative and foresight a fortune would soon be made. There was a complete electrical equip- ment, and all was ready for occupation. It could be either used as a picture house, stadium, concert hall, warehouse, place of wor- ship, business premises with shops on the ground floor and offices upstairs. It was situated in absolutely the finest place in. the town. Six years ago it fetched £3,250, and since then about £750 had been spent in improvements. It was also insured against aircraft for £3,000. The land alone, at £3 per square yard, was worth £1,650, and, besides, there was fhe valuable building on it. At £3,000 it would be a bargain. The owners wanted to sell. Everyone knew that ; bags of money, had been made there and there was the possibility, even in war time, of making a fortune out of it as a picture house. The result of his efforts were as stated above.
THE GHOSTS OF THE GREAT.

Thinking that readers would be gratified with recollections of Warrington's oldest theatre, and' the memory of " The Examiner" man being none too full, Mr. Arthur Browne, one of Warrington's most ardent theatre devotees, very kindly sat back in his chair on Thursday and indulged in most interesting reminiscences. "You ask me what I remember of the Theatre Royal?" he said. "My first recollec- tion of anything in connection with this theatre was long before it was built—when it was the Old Bandbox Theatre, which stood at right angles to Scotland-road, on part of the present site where the' Theatre Royal now stands. This would be in the year 1874 or 1875. At that time there were no sets of scenery, but small drop scenes and side wings. Mr. Brindsley Sheridan was then the proprietor, and brought down some of the most eminent actors of the day. I remember having a violin lesson from the late Mr. Rueben Manning, who was the con- ductor of the orchestra. It was on a Wednesday afternoon, and he gave it me while sitting in the orchestra itself, when Mr. Charles Matthews, the celebrated comedian, was rehearsing a young juvenile to play with him in 'My Awful Dad.' I also saw Barry Sulli- van, the celebrated tragedian, play in 'Richelieu,' Money ' and 'Richard 111.,' and some years afterwards, when the old theatre was pulled down, Mr. Henry Woods, the well- known Warrington artist, told me t)kat Mr. Sullivan had remarked to him that there was no better stage on which he liked to play than that of the old theatre. A very great attraction in those days was the Repertory Company of Mme. Beatrice, with whom was Mr. Frank Harvey, as her leading man, when crowded houses of all the most fashionable penPle in the town and district assembled the whole week through. Amongst others she played, Nosin- times ' and Ladameaux Camillia.' Mr. Charles Dillon was also a great favourite in Belphegor, the Mountebank.' Other great ' draws ' were Mr. Osmond Tearle and Mr. Edmund Tearle, .who presented different tragedies.

THE STOCK COMPANY'S SMALL STOCK. "When Mr. Sheridan could not get artistes and companies of the above class he had a stock company consisting of about six males, and three females, and sometimes they played six different pieces a week, the most popular farce of Mr. Sheridan's being, 'How To Make a Pudding.' When it was doubtful as to what to put on for Saturday night he always rehearsed either ' Hamlet ' or 'Richard lII.' Of course, the actors and actresses had to take numerous characters, and any Shakespearian student, I have since discovered, would never have known, from the way they were presented, that they were the plays written by Shakes- peare. The Stock furniture at that time con- sisted of two chairs and a table. The chairs were -not the ordinary Windsor chairs, but of bare wood. As they stood they did all right for a kitchen scene, and if they were required for a parlour act, they had to be covered with chintz. . . There were no bedroom scenes in that day'.. "One of the favourite plays of the Stock Com- pany used to be ` Bewsey Hall,' with Mr. Sheri- dan as the Watchman; others of a particularly attractive order being 'Lady Audley's Secret,' ` Miriam's Crime," and 'East Lynne,' with Sheridan as Bullock. I may add that I always maintained that it was he who created that part and not Mr. J. Pitt Hardacre, who claimed it. One of Shpridan's leading Stock men was Mr. William Henry Brougham, who, when not play- ing, followed the occupation of a house painter. I have seen him up a ladder in front of a house many a time. He is now playing in 'A Message from Mars.' I saw him not very long ago at Manchester, and found that he had lost none of his old charm. Perhaps the most successful play produced by the Stock Company was 'Conn Shaughran,' with Miss Stevenson in the princi- pal role. She was a charming lady, and used to lodge at a shop in 'Allen-street—the one on the left-hand side near the top. "Another celebrity in the Bandbox days was Miss Marriott, the tragedian, who not only played in 'Jenny Deans,' but also took the part of 'Hamlet,' and was eminently successful.

It was built with the idea of purchasing the adjoining cot- tages leading into Glasshouse-row, and the fact that these were not bought accounts for the stage being very short in depth. When the theatre was completed as it now stands, I, on the instructions of Mr. Sheridan, tried to form a company with a oapital of £B,OOO, divided into 1,600 shares of £5 each. A few well-known

townsmen—including the late Mr. Thomas Mor- ris, of Bewsey Forge; the late Mr. Daniel Jones, of Messrs. Mr. Sheridan then continued the theatre, and paid a deposit upon the purchase,of the adjoin- ing cottages to a firm of accountant% in Man- chester, but before he could find the money to carry out the plan he died. His widow carried on the business for a few years, and ultimately the mortgagees sold the property to Messrs. Johnson and Potter, who, for many years, car- ried on the theatre in conjunction with the ROyal Court. The Theatre Royal subsequently passed into other hands, "It will Anterest many to know that the Theatre Rol was principally built out of the proceeds of hard-earned money by Mr. Sheridan while touring Grelley's Money' through all the Lancashire towns, and on many Sunday noons I have seen him take out of a drawer £7O, £BO, and £9O in gold and silver as the net pro- ceeds of his week's work."

div.head: STAGE LAND.
div.p: STAGE LAND.
Royal Court.

That splendidly ingenious and up-to-date play, "The Man Who Stayed at Home," has the ad- vantage of being played at the Royal Court Theatre this week by Mr. E. Taylor Platt's com- pany, with whom is Mr. George Howard as the leading actor—Brent, the Englishman, who, amid the opprobrium of people who think he is a "slacker" because he is not interned in khaki, does most valuable work on the East Coast for the Government's Secret Service Department.

" Foyer " is not the only one who has knocked at the door of Mr. Howard's dressing-room this week, for Mr. Howard has many friends in War- rington. His past associations with the town account for this.

Especially at a time when General Smith- Dorrien is on the warpath in the theatrical world, it is interesting to observe the connection between Church and Stage in the career of Mr. Howard, for it was his father who took duty for the late Rev. W. Quekett at the Parish Church for three years. It was during this time that the son, then in his boyhood, made friends in Warrington.

Like most successful actors, he took to the stage when young, being about sixteen years of age. His first stage performance in the town was given a year or two later, when he appeared at the Theatre Royal in a popular drama enti- tled "The Dead Letter."

His theatrical career has been extremely in- teresting. He may be aptly 'described as a globe trotter, for there are few parts of the world he has not traversed, pitched his tent, as it were, and held forth in histrionic aspect. He has travelled extensively through France, Italy, Spain. Portugal and Morocco, one of the favourite pieces being "Pickwick Papers," in which he made an admirable Sam Weller. Though the play was presented in English, he remarked to melhat in the Latin countries the people know their Dickens almost as well as we do, and the play had the smoothest of passages and the best of audiences.

Until a few years ago, when he became at- tached to Mr. Taylor Platt, Mr. Howard was given to globe-trotting almost as much as a Cook's agent. He accompanied the late Wilson Barrett on ,his tours throughout America, Canada and Australia. He also went with Edward Terry on his tours to America, Canada and South Africa. Between while he has ful- filled engagements at Gibraltar, Ceylon, and Monte Carlo, and also in most of the London theatres, including the Lyric, Terry's, Prince's, Adelphi, and Drury-lane.

Generally speaking, Mr. Howard has only been concerned with the best class of plays, as may be judged from the foregoing: one does not run round the world with rubbish. Among the plays he has figured in with eminent success while-he has been with the Taylor Platt manage- ment are Bernard Shaw's You Never Can Tell" and "Arms and the Man."

The charming young lady who hands out the white feathers is a daughter of Mr. Howard, her name being Miss Duff Earle-Howard. When war broke out she was at a school near Louvain, and, having ten minutes' notice to leave, she came over to England with practically only the property she stood in. It is understood that the school has been converted into the head- quarters of the Ger Man General Staff.

Visitor,- to the Royal Court next week have a treat in store for them. That charming comedienne, Miss Madge Grey, and her power- ful company, who were here two years ago, will occupy the boards with an original potted musical comedy, "Our Kid." The piece is one unbroken round of merriment, and we expect that a long laugh, a loud laugh, indeed a long series of laughs will go round the Royal Court patrons. Miss Madge Grey com- pels laughter, making of joyousness an endless feast. She is adept at making the audience for- get trouble. 'She is original and the Wholes'ome-

He is equally successful in character studies of popular comedians. His make-up as Jack Pleasants is perfect • in every detail, and the manner in which he sings one of his unrivalled songs vividly brings to mind all the mannerisms of this eccentric entertainer.

Occupying a prominent place on the pro- gramme are Jack Win and Nora Windle, who present a breezy burlesque entitled "Railway Revelations." There is no plot, but a plethora of funny quips and comical sayings which catch on tremendously. J. E. Sutton at the piano gives an entertaining turn, which makes him a special favourite.

Fitz-Allen is seen to great advantage at the seaside, but his experiences there are peculiar and amusing. We have seldom seen nicer dancers thin the Four Cantons, presented by Mr. Alfred Canton. They are fine exponents of the "light fantastic." Bob Morrison, Scotch comedian, hammers in his jokes well, and his Warrington audiences are not unresponsive. Les Altos (from the London Alhambra) give an interesting display of herculean body balancing.

A special paragraph must be reserved for Miss Alberta Flahey, L.R.A.M., the brilliant violinist, and her tenor, Alexander Webster, A.R.A.M., who delight the audience with some beautiful music. Miss Flahey is a peculiarly gifted executant, and her rendering of "Annie Laurie," with clever melodies and double stop- ping enhancing the air, was most effective. Mr. Webster's singing of the charming ballad " Roses " was marked by much sweetness and effect.

A novelty in juggling is announced for next week, when Zellini, the Human Chimney, will appear. The Biltons will present a comedy melange, and Cole Cliffe, Yorkshire comedian, will doubtless prove as popular as formerly. De Busse is billed to play on his novelty piano- accordion, and Miss Bessie Brenne will feature her great success. "Ain't l'er Proud?" We shllll also have Clifton and Miss Daisy. one- wheel wonders, and Hector and Miss Lolktta, who are excellent equilibrists.

div.head: MUSIC HALL ARTISTE
div.p: MUSIC HALL ARTISTE
Arrested Under The Military
Service Act.

At yesterday's Borough Police Court, Alfred Cantor, who has been presenting "The Four Cantons," dancing troupe at the Hippodrome, Warrington, during the week, was charged with having failed to report himself for military ser- vice on ,the Ist November. Accused pleaded Captain McPhail, recruiting officer, informed the Bench that they ha.d to visit both house's of entertainment in 'Warrington each week in order to trace these wandering theatricals, who apparently had all the knowledge as to keeping out of the Army instead of getting into it. The defendant had been exempted on domestic cir- cumstances, until the 31st October, the certifi- cate being marked not renewable and no fur- ther. appeal .except by leave of the Tribunal. The certificate should have been returned to the local Tribunal when it ceased to be in force. Defendant had no form of exemption, and nothing to say why he should not be in the Army. By the Mayor: Defendant had attested.

Defendant explained that he was informed on the 29th October that his application had been refused, but travelled from Birmingham to Brixton on the 31st October to press his appeal on account of his wife's health.

The Mayor 'said that leave to appeal was re- fused on the 29th October, and that finally dis- posed of the matter. Defendant would not be fined, but handed over to the military escort. Captain McPhail asked their Worships to warn these theatrical people of the seriousness of this business. Hvery week visits bad to be paid to the theatres, and he thought that they had sent away twenty telegrams about these people. He and his staff and the police were engaged tracing them night after night. The only redeeming feature was that the manage- ments of the local houses gave every assistance. The Mayor whrned defaulters in strong terms.

div.head: TEACHERS' BONUS.
div.p: TEACHERS' BONUS.
Education Committee's Support
For Married Assistants.
GENERAL APPLICATION TURNED DOWN.

The Warrington Teachers' Association hav- ing made an application for, an increase of salary to all teachers on the permanent staffs receiving less than £2OO a year, the matter is to be considered by a meeting of the General Pur- poses Committee of the Town Council on Mon- day evening next. There has, however, been a discussion at the Education Committee, with the result that an expression of opinion that a special war bonus of £lO per annum shall be paid to all married assistant masters in receipt of not more than £165. Ai their meeting last Monday evening the Education Committee had that recom- mendation before them, it having been passed by the School Management Committee. At the outset the Mayor* said that the Town Clerk had suggested .that the resolution which now appeared on the minutes might be with- drawn with a view of the whole question of a war bonus to Corporation employes being dis- cussed by the General Purposes Committee of the Town Council on Monday evening next. At the present time those in receipt of £2 or under per week were enjoying a bonus. He (the Mayor) thought it only right that the teachers' case should be considered with the others next Monday. While not resisting the suggestion that the resolution of the School Management Com- mittee should be withdrawn, under the circumstances, Mr. John Upson pointed out that almost every other authority was dealing with the teachers separately from the other employes of the Corporation. Liver- pool, Manchester, St. Helens and Oldham had all dealt with the teachers separately. Mr. Edwin Plinston hoped that the with- drawal would not mean that the General Pur- poses Cotamittee would grant less than what the School Management Committee had recom- mended, for if the position of the teachers of Warrington were submitted to any commission dealing with salaries they would get a very different award from what had been suggested, male and female as well. He hoped that by the minute being sent back the position of the teachers was not going to be jeopardised. Having been granted leave to speak again, Mr. Upson remarked that that committee had saved a very considerable sum indeed because the men whq had enlisted had been replaced by women, *ho were paid on the women's scale, and if that resolution became operative the committee would still have a considerable balance in hand out-of what was being saved. Somehow or other it seemed a little sordid that, by a committee or anyone, money should be made out of the fact that men were serving their King and country. _ _

NATIONALISATION OR PROHIBI-

Sir,—The meeting at the Warrington Working Men's Mission last ,Monday week on the question of liquor nationalisation, revealed a decided cleavage of opinion among the tee- totalists and advocates of prohibition, which resulted in some dangerous admissions on the part of the nationalisation faction. -Whereas Mr. W. A. Platt was strongly opposed to drink nationalisation, and frankly declared for pro- hibition, Councillor Roberts, in urging national- isation, incautiously admitted that "the ex- treme temperance men's influence upon publie opinion was practically nil," and, that nationalisation was only to be a half-way house to prohibition, for which public opinion was not ripe." While firmly convinced of the un- desirability of prohibition, I, nevertheless, can find more sympathy with Mr. Platt's candid and open advocacy thereof than with the Jesuitical propaganda of the teetotalist nationalisers, who as Councillor Roberts' unguarded statements prove—only advocate nationalisation as a means to the. same end—compulsory total abstinence: If, as -Councillor Roberts says, the public pay no heed to the prohibitionists, how does he expect them to listen to the nationalisation scheme, when; as he himself admits, that scheme itself is only the pill of prohibition carefully guilded ?—Yours, /Lc.; S. SIMPSON. November 13th, 1916.

div.head: SUFFOCATED.
div.p: SUFFOCATED.
Piece Of Tripe Causes Death Of
Widow.

The strange facts of a death by misadventure tianspired at an inquest by Deputy Coroner F. A. Jones, on the body of Sarah Ellen Ham widow, 65 years, who died suddenly at • her residence, 42, Dalton Bank, Warrington, on Saturday afternoon. Joseph Boardman, blacksmith's striker, same address, stated that deceased, a distant relative, was the widow of the late James Hayes park- 'keeper, and acted as his housekeeper. Witness came home to dinner on Saturday, and Mrs. Hayes was preparing some fried tripe and onions. She was cutting the tripe into pieces, and the onions and some of the tripe were cook- ing in the pan. He saw her go into the back kitchen and heard her vomiting. She came out again and pointed to her throat. Witness sat her down op a chair and went for assistance. Dr. Andersdn, Manchester-road, came, and said that she was dead. Deceased had false teeth, and when he (witness} looked into-her mouth they Wveared to be in their proper ;place. The Coroner: There was some •tripe found, in her throat ?—Yes. _ _

The Coroner: Like a good housewife, she was trying it to see if it was cooked. Dr. Anderson said that the cause of death was suffocation. He did not find any tripe in the throat, but he had not made a post mortem examination. He found the roof of the false teeth, lying at the back of the throat. The Coroner: Then she ,died from suffocation, probably caused by a piece of tripeF—Yes. In elderly 'people death in such a case would be remarkably quick. The jury returned a verdict of death by mis- adventure—that Mrs. ''Hayes was suffocated; probably from a piece of tripe lodging in the larynx.

Canon Willis, rural dean, presiding over a fair attendance of clergy. The speaker replied to three questions: "Why should we keep Sunday? How should we keep Sunday? How can the, clergy best fulfil their obligations ?" Had they been too strictly Sabbatarian in their demands, he asked further. He felt that they had rather demanded almost too much, and they had been satisfied with much too little. Having shown why Sunday should be observed, he pointed out that the Holy Com- munion should be the principal portion of the service, and that Matins were preparatory and leading up to the Sacrament. The latter por- tion of Sunday might be used for instructing children, and the evening service should. be rather given to instruction than exhortation. Privided then that the claims of worship had been attended to, they could rightly sanction healthy recreation for the individual taste. One would prefer reading, another, a bicycle ride, and 'for another an outdoor game. In itself anything that was right on a week-day was right on a Sunday, provided it did not destroy the atmosphere of the day. Saturday evening had also much to do with the proper recognition of Sunday. It should be kept quietly as a preparation for the Lord's Day. (Hear, hear.) The President agreed as to the observation with reference to Saturday nights. Rev.. B. E. Taylor said that when the choir remained during the communion service it had the result of making more members of the con- gregation remain also. With regard to recrea- tion, man's first duty was to love God, and if he loves recreation on the Lord's Day he cannot love God.

Rev. A. M. Mitchell also joined in,the desire for a quiet Saturday night to prepare for the next day's service. Rev. C. Moore, Earlestown, had come to see great spiritual benefit_ in evening communion. _

Rev. W. Greenwood, Earlestown, deprecated anything being said or dOne to encourage the desecration of God's day. If they thought that a man who had communicated was at liberty to go and golf and cycle or play football or any- thing else, then they gave him a liberty which he would very quickly turn into licence. (Hear, hear.)

The Rector of Liverpool, in reply, said:that in his remarks about recreation he did • not in- tend in any way that they should authorise or encourage anything like' desecration- of Sunday. He was rather thinking of the person who was hard at office or manual labour all the week and who had nothing like an opportunity for a cycle ride except on Sunday. (Hear, hear.)

div.p: WATCH THE GERMANS.

The speaker at the evening conference was the Rev. S. A. J. Barrett, vicar of St. Ann's, Liverpool, who dealt with "The duty of • the Church after the war." He said that free will had been given to man to use in a moral direc- tion, and the war showed that they had used free will in a wrong direction. Germany had used it for an exaltation of might, an exaltation of war. They should evolve the fruits of vic- tory not through the bloodiness of war, but through the beauties of peace and to see that the spirit of self-sacrifice, of unselfishness, that the spirit of working shoulder to shoulder should be maintained when all the horrors of war had passed away. (Hear, hear.) •What should be their attitude to the German when war was over was often asked, but could any- one tell him what the condition of affairs would be then? They should wish the Germans well and that the good parts of them would be de- veloped and the evil eradicated; yet he would not trust the German very much but keep his eye on him. (Laughter, and applause.) They were told that the-- Church was a failure—but those failures existed before the war, and he instanced the fact of very small church attend- ances in Liverpool. The Church, he contended, should look after the better training of its clergy iri.order that-they might be able to deal effectively with the men who returned from the war; and services ought to be arranged that would meet the necessities of these men.

div.head: Church and Labour.
div.p: The Church and Labour.

• The Church should also take a definite stand in -regard to Labour. :When it was found that three per cent. of the population were receiving incomes of £7oo'a year and over; nine per cent. of the population with incomes of from £l6O to £7OO, and eighty-eight per cent. of the population were poor, it showed a system which stood self- condemned. (Applause.) He went on to urge that they should have Church Schools for their children. When the Roman Catholics could have them, why not they? They should also take care that the wages earned by women would not be lowered after the war, and that they should endeavour to establish a healthy state of morals in the land. They had a glorious message in this time of stress to give to their people: the old faith to proclaim, and which was morally satisfying. Rev. A. M. Mitchell asked if the drink traffic was to remain the same after the war as before, and were profiteers to be allowed to retain the huge profits they had annexed? Would soldiers receive what was 'due to them in the way of pensions? div.p: CHRISTMAS PUDDINGS FOR THE TRENCHES.

"The Examiner" Fund for providing Plum Puddings on Christmas Day for our soldiers on all the fighting fronts in the world now amounts to £7,7 3s. sd. It should be borne in mind that the War Office have asked the "Daily News" and the "Daily Telegraph" to raise all the money necessary. to provide a ration of plum pudding for 3,000,000 men, and that " The Examiner" is helping those two newspapers to raise the necessary £60,000. Puddings sent by private persons or un- authorised bodies will stand in the way of the flelivery of other parcels .more urgently needed, and the War Office specially request the public not to double upon the work we and our contemporaries have 'undertaken. Many thousands of pounds are still required if no one is 'to be left unserved on Christmas Day, and we hope our readers will continue to respond as liberally as :they have done up to the present. To illustrate the spirit in which the work of collection. is being carried out, we would point to the £lO 13s. 7d. taken on .the Football Ground last Saturday by 'a body of young ladies entaged. by the Alliance ,Box Co. Adult School Member Wounded, But
Never " %Vent Down."
Corporal Harold Biddall, K. 0.5.8., 53, Lan- caster-street, writing to the President of the

Sankey Bridges Adult School, of which he was one of the original members, says he is still in good health. "We are," he states, "out of the trenches at present, just a mile or two behind, in canvas tents. The tents 4re all right, but the weather is not—it has rained every day for the last fifteen days, and 'we have had some of it in the trenches. My word! Talk about a Mile a minute; you could not do a Mile an hour up to the knees in pure mud. At plenty of trenches you had to risk it and walk on top or you would have got stuck. . . . We. have done our share of the scrapping since we came here three months yesterday; we got ten days about six miles back, and then up and 'into it again. We have had a good few prisoners—we had the record for one day; noes° bad? . . . Mrs. Butler, 5, Lord Nelson-street, has re- ceived the following letter from Second-Lieut. E. H. Llewellyn, Dorsetshire Regiment, con- cerning her husband, Private Stephen 'Butler, of the same regiment, who has been killed. The letter stated, "I was close to your husband when he was hit by fragments of a shell which burst close to us, and he was badly wounded in the upper part of the right leg and the lower part of the back. div.head: PRISONERS' PARCELS.
div.p: PRISONERS' PARCELS.
Voluntary Helpers To Pack Them Urgently Needed.
To the Editor of "The Examiner."

Sir,—We should esteem it a favour it you would allow us to make an appeal through the columns of your valued newspaper. Under the new scheme for the relief of prisoners of war of the South Lancashire Regiment, the pack- ing and dispatching parcels have been greatly increased. All food parcels for these men have now to be sent through our own local organisa- tion at the Parr Hall, and very much more voluntary help is needed than has been hitherto necessary.

We are not at, liberty to state how many prisoners of war are interned in Germany be- longing to the South Lancashire Regiment, but :we may call to mind that during .the retreat from Mons dur men acquitted ttemselves gallantly, and played a magnificent part in that most critical engagement.

Many of our prisoners have been interned since October, 1914, and we have now to face the fact that regular food parer.", must be sent to them, and tliat it must be done by our own local organisatien. Under the new scheme each man will receive three parcels per fortnight, which will . ensure them full and adequate nutriment, and a regular supply of bread will he sent either from here or Switzerland and eopenhagen. The work of the present organisa- tion has, therefore, been nearly trebled, and we shall require at least thirty conscientious and reliable helpers.

It is hoped that all the necessary packing and dispatching will be done during the daytime in order to save the expense of lighting, &c. An appeal, therefore, is made.' for help to those who can give the necessary time, whether ladies or gentlemen. The days for packing and dis- patching parcels for December will be the 4th, 6th, 13th, 18th, 22nd and 29th, the dates for subsequent months will be arranged later. Those who can help are asked to write to the nor. Secretary sQf the Regimental Care Com- mittee, stating ffie hours they can give. The -vliole of this work is now of great importance, inasmuch as the welfare Of our men interned in Germany is now under our care, and it is nil done under the authOrity of the British Red Cross Society and the -Order of St. John of Je,liqalem in England.
We have every-assurance that the parcels dis- tched to our men, actually reach their ation, and that the serve the Purpose for which they are sent.

Signed: PETER PEACOCK (Ikfavor), Colonel J. A. MOGGRIWE, 0/C South Lancs. Regt. Rev. /RV/YE LISTER, Hon. Sec. Regimental Care Committee for Prisoners of War of the South Lancashire Regiment, Parr Hall, Warrington, 22nd November, 1916.

div.head: TURK'S DESTINY.
div.p: THE TURK'S DESTINY.
AAA' He Be Kicked Out Of Ettrope,?

Continuing his lectures on "Constantinople; its history' and art," at the Co-operative Hall on Saturday evening, Mr. J. E. Phythian spoke on "The Mahornetan City." Mahometanism when it started, he said, was in the midst of polytheism, and to-day, in some parts of Africa it made quicker .progress. than Christianity. The Mahornetans had behaved very badly in Armenia and Bulgaria, but we, even' in Christianity, had not been without bad be- haviour. At home and abroad .there had been a great deal of persecution in the propagation of the Gospel by force. Referring to the pro- gress of the Turk, the lecturer said it was Mahomet the conqueror who took Constanti- nople. Thereafter, attacks were made on their Christian neighbours. In 1456 the conqueror's armies made attacks on Belgrade, • but were arrested. In 1775 they conquered the Crimea. They also annexed Greece, .and Europe began' to tremble. But Mahomet the conqueror died, and Europe sent up, a sigh of relief. His grand- son, however, succeeded him and annexed Syria and Egypt, while Belgrade was at last captured. The Turks were now ruling almost the whole of the Christian' population of the Eastyrn Empire, and they also ruled in Hungary until the end of the; 'seventeenth century. The greatest power of the Turks was in the sixteenth century, and Arabia, Cyprus and Crete fell into their hands, but in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries their power began to wane. In conclusiOn, the lecturer, said the Turk was now the ." sick man" of Europe, and the question was, "What is goiag to happen to him?" "Was he going to be turned out of Europe, or were the Germans and Austrians going to bolster him up.again?"

A Happy Throng.

Sir Arthur and Lady Crosfield are spending a few days in Warrington, and last evening they visited, together with the Mayoress (Mrs. Peacock), a children's party held in the. John Crosfield Memorial Hall, pnder the auspices of the Women's Liberal Association, the pro- ceeds going to provide woollen comforts for local soldiers. As all the refreshments were given, the funds benefited considerably. Over 200 children attended and enjoyed themselves thoroughly in the patriotically decorated rooms. The proceedings opened with a grand march past (to' Tipperary!), and afterwards various kinds of entertainment were indulged in—dancing (the polka was a great favourite), musical chairs, rings, blind man's buff, &c. The music was supplied by Miss Vera Jones and Mr. G. S. Pendlebury. Lady Crosfield danced a polka with some of the girls. On her seeking a partner from among the boys they were either too shy or unacquainted with the brisk and fascinating measure, for none •came forward. As an interlude, Sir Arthur and Lady Cros- field made crisp and happy speeches, wishing the children the best of enjoyment through- out the evening, and the guests cheered them rousingly. The arrangements were in the hands of the Hon. Secretary (Mrs. E. Osborne), and the committee of the War Sewing Class. Mr. T. H. Edwards and Mr. J. Percival acted as M.C.'s.

Out on a plain, over which I have crossed many times, on my way, to the trenches, • amongst the graves of our soldiers, is one with a simple cross of wood at the head; and written on a piece of tin are the following words :
Here lies the body of an unknown British Soldier. .
Out on a plain, where warriors feet still tread, Where victories.havre been won in battle zone, And Britain' 6 sons have freely fought and blO, In solitude a comrade's body lies, by all un- known.
'Tis but a simple cross, which marks his lonely
grave, ' And no inscription bears upon the pike of wood; • But 'tis enough for us to know his life he gave To ,•,ave his friends, and prove the (greater love.
No sculptor shall for him, in marble white, Carve out some letters, that it may be known To comrades, as they pass the lonely sight, The honoured name and regiment that he had borne.
But he is known to the great God of all, Who cloth the records of His children keep, And counteth e'en the sparrows when they fall, Unseen by man, to earth in deadly sleep.

BIBLE AND UNITY.
Mr. C. E. Parker On Denomina- tional Divisions.

The Holy Bible as a force in uniting religious denominations and as a comfort to those who are faced with questions of life and death in such large numbers to-day, was dwelt upon in an interesting manner at the annual meeting of the Warrington branch of the British and Foreign Bible Society, held in the Co-operative Hall on Thursday evening. First, the increased interest taken locally in the society was reflected in the increased sub- scriptions, last year the sum being 0f.;57, and this year £7O, Mr. Segar Owen, the hon. treasurer, expressing the hope that next year the sum would reach three figures. Remarking that the society recognised no creeds or divisions, the Chairman (Mr. C. E. Parker) said he was very glad to feel that the society was a bond of union, binding them in loyalty to their common Master, but he could not help feeling that in regard to Warrington the unity was not so apparent or real as it ought to be at their meetings. Many repre- sentative Christian men, whom they would like to see, appeared not to be enthusiastic, and he could not understand it. He had heard one reason for it, which he was not going to express, because it seemed to be altogether inapt. But if it were the real reason why a number of those men did not support them or give approval to the work of the society, it seemed about as sensible as if, at the beginning of the war, Britain had declined to fight alongside the French because they had been against us at Waterloo. (Applause.) If there ever were a time when all Christian people should unite it was now, for it was due to the materialism of Germany that the war had come about. Spirituality was essential to progress. The Bible was an enormous factor in making for righteous- ness, and if there were more unity among Christian peoples they would make better head- way in that respect. - He wished that every year the Bible Sotiety's meeting would be regarded as a great rally of members of all denomination!. (Applause.) The Rev. Arthur Taylor, of London, one of the general .secretaries of the society, delivered an interesting address, in which he pointed out that the Bible had not only survived the war, but now stood more firmly entrenched in the lives of the people than ever. No kook like the Bible had proved so sympathetic and consoling, and it was regarded as the supreme Book ot the world. The extent of the work of the society might'be judged from the facts that, apart from the supplies they were sending all over the world, they had forwarded 5.000.000 Bibles to soldiers during the war and 300,000 New Testa- ments to 1,200 hospitals. Votfs of thanks were accorded on the proposal of the Rev. T. Dring (Wallasey), seconded by the Rev. W. T. Derry. Those present included the Revs. B. Percival, A. J. Morton, T. T. James, Ef. Ogden, and Mr. J. C. Holland.

div.head: TOWN'S OLDEST SERVANT.
div.p: TOWN'S OLDEST SERVANT.
Death Of Mr. John Booth,
Ex-Road Foreman.

Warrington has lost another of its old and highly respected residents, and also its oldest ex-Corporation servant, in the person of Mr. John 6Booth, who passed away at his home, 45, Bewsey-street, on Wednesday afternoon, at the age of eighty-seven years. He enjoyed fairly good health until a little over two months ago, when he took to his bed, and remained there until the time of his death. After serving an apprenticeship as a stone- mason with a Warrington firm, he joined the Corporation in that capacity in 1853. His good services were rewarded in 1875, when he was appointed road foreman, to be followed in 1905 by an appointment as surveyor for private street work. He acted in this capacity until he entered upon his retirement a few years ago, having been a member qf the Corporation for sixty years and eight mohths. A staunch Liberal, he was a member of the Liberal Club, where he was well known and respected. Often he was to be seen at the Club, having a quiet dame of cards or a chat. As a tribute to him the flag was flown at half-mast on Wednesday. He belonged to the Parish Chu,rch' Choir about seventy years ago, and that hit memory had remained perfectly active to the last may be judged from the fact that during his illness he spoke of a hymn which he sang as a chor- ister se many years ago. Accident In The Dark.—Mr. Jeffrey Bowyer, son of Mr. Joseph Bowyer, Warrington-road, had an unfortunate accident in Horsemarket- street, Warrington, last - Saturday night. Whilst going to the Central Station to catch a train home he stumbled and fell in the darkened thoroughfare, sustaining severe con- tusions on the chin and eyebrows, which left him in a dazed condition. Fortunately his brother was with him and attended to his im- mediate requirements, and saw him safely home.

Home From The War.—Driver Sam Spark, A.S.C., son of Mr. Sparks, Chapel-road, is home on leave from the Western Front after sixteen months' arduous duties in taking supplies up to the fighting line. A Penketh Tannery employe prior to the beginning of the war, he very soon answered his country's call, for he enlisted early in September, 1914. After ten months' training he crossed the Channel for more serious work. Two brothers are also serving. Lewis is still in Belfast Hospital re- covering from wounds received in action, and John is at present training in the South of England. • Prize Band At Liverpool—At an instrumental quartet contest held in the Rushworth Hall, Liverpool, last Saturday, the Penketh Tannery Prize Brass Band tried hard for the premier position, but found themselves relegated to the fifth place. As twenty-six sets competed, it was no mean achievement to be in the first five. Mr. A. Gray, conductor of the Manchester Pro- fessional Military; Band, acted as judge. The prizes were awarded as under :-1, Wingates Temper- ance; 2, Foden's Motor Works; 3, Wingates Temperance; 4, Foden's Motor Works; 5, Pen- keth Tannery. div.p: KHAKI BREAD.
Best For The Body If Not Attractive To The Eye.

The opening of the New Year will see the introduction of Standard Bread,. and Warring- ton has already had, some experience of it. For a while some five or six years ago the loaves of slightly brownish hue were bought and eaten. by many, who assured themselves that their stomachs would gain an advantage at the ex- pense of attractiveness to the eyesight, and such is the fact, for it is perhaps generally admitted by the medical profession that the nutriment in Standard Bread will probably con- tain a greater quantity of gluten and fattening element. The great change will be merely from an uesthetic point of view, and it is rather a curious thing that the majority of people de- velop an artistic taste where a white loaf is con- cerned—the whiter it is the more they enjoy it, or think they do. It is hard to foretell what the effect will be on confectionery and fancy breads. These dainties will not be perhaps so alluring as heretofore, but if the sugar supply is not seriously diminished, they will probably retain their palatable peculiarities. We may be certain on one point and that is, an eager competition on the part of milling firms to turn out the best and most' attractive article possible, while complying strictly with the Government regulations. The best-looking, might one say? the most fair and handsome, will secure the best market.

LOCAL FACTS AND FANCIES.
By CRITIC.
During the past week our worthy Clerk of the Council has been asking for road repairers for work in France. ,
To pave the new way to Berlin, I surmise.

I noticed that the age limit was 50 years, which gives a chance for those so anxious to do their bit that were just over military age. No doubt by this time the worthy Clerk will have his book full with the names of these anxious men.
Regarding the dark weather and the lighting restrictions, I overheard an old gentleman say the other day that "This should have come about .fifty yeas ago."
He had just collided with one of the other sex, and the apology he uttered served as -in intrOduction.
I jokingly reminded him that "every dog has its day."
'Yes," he said, " and there's life in the old birds yet."

To avoid these collisions some people think that ere long it will be compulsory to carry a headlight. Why not a red rear light also?—Fastened on the coat and worked by an electric battery from the pocket. _ _
_ Even couples could hardly object to this, for when they get out of danger's way—switch off the light, and all's well. •
, The proceeds of the sale. of work held at the Wesleyan Church last Wednesday week were somewhere about £52. , .
Recently at this Church there seems to have been some comment as to ,who will fill the organist's chair recently vacated by Mr. Stanley lanes.
I can now say on good authority that this important position will be filled by Miss A. Finch. And she will commence her new duties/to- morrow.,
I notice with interest that some of our large grocery firms are utilising women labour for delivering orders.
And right good " horsemen " they make. I should not be surprised if our Council jump at the same remedy for "scarcity of labour." Women are now doing their bit in almost every sphere of life.
The Oughtrington Platoon of Volunteers held a hot-pot supper at the. Farmers' Arms last Wednesday night.
And for a time forgot about the torture of "platoon drill," &e., and gave the inner man a thorough "bust up."

Private Fred Percival Well Again.--.-PriVate Fred Percival, reported ill in a dental hospital a few weeks ago, writing to his wife at Moston- street, says: "I am in the 'pink' once again. I have not yet received .the cigarettes you sent to the regiment, but I expect to get them any time now, as my brother Sam promised to send all my mails on to me. I was more than pleased to hear that your brother Arthur is getting all right again. I expect he will be coming home on the usual ten days' leave before olng. Give my best respects to ,all; and tell them to buck up, for we shall all be home before long." The Arthur referred to is Private Arthur Statham, who was severely wounded some time ago.

div.head: " BLUESTONE " DEPARTS.
div.p: " BLUESTONE " DEPARTS.
Two Popular Brookfield Soldiers Leave
-Amid Pleasant Scenes.

Private Jack .Blackett, of the Durham Light Infantry, coMmonly known to his hospital chums and residents as "Bluestone," and Corporal Shedd, of the Machine Gun Section; two popular Brookfield soldiers, left the hos- pital early last Wednesday morning on the usual ten days' leave prior to rejoining their units. Shortly after seven a.m. our repre- sentative was startled to hear a noise coming from the direction of the Brookfield Military Hospital. Thinking something unusual was taking place he cautiously approached, and ' there found the two departing soldiers being given a right loyal send-off at the hands of their 'fellow .patients. Cheer after cheer rent the air as the two heroes made their final preparations, and as they gave their final :tandshake at the hospital door they stood under a novel kind of archway made from the crutches of their maimed 4comrades. Both" soldiers seemed to realise the situation, and as they took their leave one could notice the restrained emotions on the faces of both men. Such scenes as these cannot but leave tender memories in the hearts of all soldiers for the old village, with which the great war brought them into contact.

div.head: PRIVATE JACK RAVENSCROFT.
div.p: PRIVATE JACK RAVENSCROFT.
Hopes To See A Bull Fight.

Private Jack Ravenscroft, of the Cheshire Regiment, one of our local soldiers, who is at present stationed somewhere in- India, writing to his brother at Oldfield-road, Statham, says:— " There have been very heavy rainfalls here these last few days, and when rain does come I can assure you you never know when it is going, to stop—the ground fairly shakes. ,Things are pretty exciting at times; for. instance, there is a bull fight to-night and I hope, with a little luck, to be able to see it. I enclose some photo- graphs of Mesopotamia, several views of towns and outside places I have been in. You will find them very interesting." Private Jack Ravenscroft was one of " Derby's " first men. He joined the Cheshire Regiment; and wag drafted out to Mesopo- tamia in May, eventually being sent to. India. During all the time he has been overseas, up to a short time ago he had not received a single letter from England, although an average of two or three letters a week has been sent out to him. He has been in hospital twice with sunstroke. During his period of active service he has had no fewer, than six different com- plaints, and knows what it is to be without water for three days. His home address is Moston-street. Newfields He is a goldbeater employed by Wm. Wright and Sons, goldbeaters and refiners, of Newfields.

div.head: LYMM IN WAR-TIME.
div.p: LYMM IN WAR-TIME.
The Folly Of The Electric Flashlight.
By S.D.M.

Now that we are feeling the effects of the lighting restrictions, and the village is in absolute darkness it is up to us to see that people are not put to any ramie inconvenience than is absolutely necessary under the pro- visions of the Order. It is with this view in mind that I take up the pen to attack those people who are apt to make use, and in cases abuse, the advantages of the pocket flash- light. Lymm at the best of times was always poorly lighted;, and I think that you will agree with me when I say that at the present time no village, town, or city, whether on'the coast or inland, could be in any way more affected than Lymm. Does anyone ever go out of doors in the evening now and remain out for any specified time , without being called upon to tender at least a dozen apologies? Let me take your minds back to last Sunday evening. Everywhere was black—pitch black, 'nothing could be seen, and the only warning you had that anyone was approaching was the tramp of feet; even this in the case of rubber heels was very difficult to locate. Wise- people carried lanterns, and .unthoughtful ieople resorted to the use of pocket flashlights, and—shall I say?— the wisest of all remained indoors. Nevertheless those who were out were subject to a great deal of annoyance by those unthoughtful youths— and, in many cases, girls—who carried these unseen dangers—pocket flashlights. By a little forethought this evil can be avoided. Curiosity is really the chief cause of all the mischief. At various intervals when you were Talking down the dark streets, straining your eyes to comprehend your surroundings, you were blinded by a sudden flash of light which seemed to come from nowherC, but really Came from the flashlight -carried by one of these mis- chievous boys or girls. For several minutes you were blind, not knowing where you were, and if by chance a vehicle . was approaching you put it down to good luck if you were not on the casualty list. Picture yourself a cyclist in the same predicament. A man could easily lose control of his machine when suddenly blinded in this way, and 4ash to a horrible death. Let the thoughtless people take a little sound advice —if they want to use a flashlight, let them use it in reason, not abuse it, or better still, leave it alone, and use the ordinary hand lamp.

div.p: PADGATE.

Musical Evening At The Wesley Guild.—A musical evening provided entertainment for the members of the Padgate Wesley Guild on Thursday. The first item was a chorus, "Britannia." Two songs, "The Vicar of Bray," by Miss M. Ball, and "John Bull," by Dr. Bennett, were well rendered. The " Marseillaise " was then sung by all present. Miss J. Stewart sang "Bonnie Mary of Argyle," which was followed by a recitation, "A Prayer for our Soldiers," by Miss A. Meredith. "My Ain Fireside," by Miss J. Ward, was very well sung, followed by a chorus, "March Of the Men of Harlech." Another chorus, "The British Grenadiers," and two songs, "My Bonnie is Over the Ocean," by Mrs. Bate, and "The Maple Leaf," by Miss A. Ball. The accompanists on the piano were Mrs. Bate and Miss E. Woods, .with Dr. Bennett on the violin. A competition organised by Miss E. London and Miss L. Wright, caused some merriment, and on the announcement of the result the prizes went to Miss South (1), Mr. Plinston (2), Mrs. Morton (3), and Mrs. J. Bennett (4). Mr. W. E. Mins- ton thanked the artistes for their services.

War Relief Society.—An American tea, or- ganised by the committee of the Padgate War Relief Society, was held in the Wesley Hall last Saturday. Each person was asked to give an article and buy one, the result - being that :a large and varied assortmeat of articles were offered for sale. The doors were opened at three o'clock, and two hours after this time there was very little left for late-comers to purchase. The Provision Stall was in charge of Mrs. Haddock and Miss Smith, along with Mrs. Newton, Mrs. Plinston, and Miss Eaglesfield; and Fancy Stall of Miss Turner, Mrs., Morton, and Mrs. Walsh. Refreshments were served in the Guild Room, these, along with the Confec- tionery Stall, being in the hands of Mrs. J. Bennett, Miss Jackson, Miss Mason, Mrs. Duckworth, Mrs. Lunt, Miss Birtles, Mrs. Ezard, Mrs. Howard and Mrs. Denham; whilst Mrs. Grounds and Mrs. Toft were responsible for the making of the tea. A varied musical programme was provided throughout the after- noon by Dr. Bennett (violin), Miss Birtles (violoncello), Miss Phyllis Nixon (soloist) and Miss C. Smith, of Warrington (accompanist). The proceeds, which were in aid of sending comforts to soldiers who have joined the colours, were as follows :—Provision Stall, ..t8 10s. 9d.• Fancy Stall, -a 12s. 4d., including Is.. subscription from' Mr. Gorton; refresh- ments and confectionery, £ll 13s. 10d.; total, .R2B 16s. 11d. In addition there were two sub- sCriptions of a guinea each from Mr. J. Hough- ton and Mr. Percy Bennett. There was a good number present and the result was most satis- factory.

Missionary Anniversary.—Special sermons in aid of Foreign Missions were preached in the Wesleyan Church last Sunday by the Rev. E. Morton, of Bradford. The annual missionary- meeting was held on Tuesday evening, pre- sided over by Mr. E. Lunt, and supported by the- Rev. F. Hudson, of Warrington (late" of the Transvaal), who was the speaker for the evening, the Rev. B. Morton, and the Rev. A. J. Morton. In the annual report, read' by the Rev. A. J. Morton, it was stated that the year 1915 had been a year of strain and disorganisa- tion. In France services were practically dis- continued owing to shortage of ministers, and, in Italy the religious cause was greatly affected by the war. Good progress had been made in India, Africa and China, which was very gratifying. Out of the sum of X148,398,_ col- lected from the various circuits in Great 'Bri- tain for missionary work, the Liverpool circuit had subscribed .k 10,431 the Warrington cir- cuit, .t 331 12s. 2d., Padgate's contribution being <R39 3s. 10d.

The Rev. F. Hudson, who was well received, .said he was pleased to say he' represented one part of the missionary field which was showing an advance year after year, this advance being more marked and steady since the Boer War. There wae still a great deal of pioneer work to be done in this part, but the work was now getting in the secondary state. In the Northern Transvaal the population was very sparse and it was very' difficult work educating the native in the ethics of Christianity owing to his having centuries of barbarism behind him. In South Transvaal, the greater part Of the work was to counteract the forces of evil which were at work, especially the liquor traffic. In the Eastern Transvaal the work was more or less- wild work, similar to the Northern part. In addition to native work the missionaries did a good work .among the white people, principally in raising derelicts who have gone, astray in the Colonies. The natives were very generous "in giving, and to- day the Church was growing stronger and stronger. The work was very hard and costly, some parts being healthy and others very un- healthy; but whilst the toll was very great on those that go, it was infinitely :worth while. . A vote of' thanks to the speaker was pro- posed by the Rev. A. J. Morton, and 'readily assented to by all present.

div.head: IN THE COURTS.
div.p: IN THE COURTS.
A PRIVILEGE ABUSED.
Railway Employes' Ticket Regulations Broken.

An unusual case was heard at the Borough. Police Court on Thursday, when Mrs. Mary Anne Heesom, 8, St. Mary-street, was prosecuted by Superintendent Hogg, Cheshire Lines Com- mittee, for travelling to Manchester from War- rington on the 19th October, and to Liverpool from Warrington on the 28th October, without paying her fare, and with using on each oc,casion a. third-class inter-change privilege ticket made out for- the•wife of her son, Thomas Heesom, witli intent to defraud the company. Thomas Heesom was charged with complicity in the alleged fraud. Both defendants denied the charge. Mr. T. S. Steel, solicitor, represented the Cheshire Lines Committee.

Briefly, the facts for the prosecution showed that Heesom, being a goods guard on the L. and N.-W. Railway had certain privileges, as Ek railway servant, for travelling over other lines. An application was signed, presented to the thead of his department, who issued an order. The latter was then produced at the booking office of the other railway and tickets issued at quarter fare. On the 19th October Heesom made application for two inter-change 'tickets on the Cheshire Lines Railway to Man- chester for himself and his wife, and on the 128th October a similar application for a ticket from Warrington to Liverpool for his wife. Two 'women, one the female defendant, travelled to Manchester with the first-mentioned tickets and here, owing to a slight difference in the forma- tion of the tickets—one being for a man and the other for a woman—the holders were stopped and questioned. Tie second female Stated that she was Heesom's wife, when, as a: matter of fact, Mr. Steel•explained, Mrs. ,Heesom. had been separated from her husbaiid for five years, and would give evidence to th:s effect. On the 28th October Heesom's mother travelled to Liverpool with the ticket that Heesom had obtained for his wife. When questioned sub- sequently by Detective Hewitt, of the ,railway police, the female defendant insisted that she had• travelled with her son's wife on both occaMons, and Heesom himself said his wife would be a liar if she stated otherwise—or said that she had been separated from him for five years. Evidence having been given in detail by the company's officials. Mrs.' Clara Heesom, wife of the male defend- ant, in reply to Mr. Steel, stated that she lived with her mother at 99, Sharp-street, Warring- ton. She did not liv6 at defend9nt's address. She had been separated from her husband five years ago, and lived apart from him, since then. She had never been to either Manchester or Livarpool with himself or his mother, and had ever visited either place herself. She had never lived at 8, St. Mary-street, and her husband had never procured any privilege tickets for her. Heesom, in reply to the Clerk of the Court, said he had no question to ask his wife; and both defendants intimated that they had no statement to make to the Court.

The Chairman (Mr. John Rymer Young) said this was a very serious ease: if such a practice continued it might result-in the company with- drawing concessions from people who would use them honestly.- The ,defendants had aggravated the case by positive untruthfulness. They would each be fined 20s. in each case and the advocate's fee would be £2 2s. Fines and costs amounted to £6 2s.

Throwing back the great front door of the Powell mansion Blair Stanleigh darted from the vestibule and around the house to the back, closely followed by Vivian Marston and the shaking master of the mansion. There beneath the high window lay the battered body of Frank Durand, physician and crook—the erstwhile King of Diamonds. His neck was broken, but the grasp of his right hard had relaxed and The Diamond from the Sky was gone. " We must think of what account we can give of this," whispered Vivian, the quickest witted of the trio. Then she spoke as though directly to John Powell. "Did you see the struggle? It must have been De Vaux who killed him." Arthur had been too dazed from the effect of the sleeping powder that Durand had secretly adminis- tered earlier in the night to have anything but a confused recollection of what had really occurred. Then Blair spoke up. "I heard the fight in your room and rushed in," -he said. "De Vaux was beat- ing Durand with a. loaded stick, I think. Yes, here it is," and he picked up the ugly weapon from where it lay beside the dead man. "Then De Vaux rushed past me and escaped with the diamond after pushing Durand from the window." It was near daybreak and the noise and confu- sion had awakened the servants. Parker, the butler, always devoted to his master, appeared first, and helped to lead the shaken John Powell back into the house. He was too nervously confused to remember that the front door had been bolted and that Blair had opened it. He could only vaguely substantiate the story to the police and newspapers that Durand had been beaten and thrown from the bedroom window by thugs, who had stolen the diamond that John Powell had purchased at the bankrupt sale of Santley Circus. Meanwhile De Vaux had found shelter in the grey, of dawn at Signora Solari's cafe, La Bella Napoli, rousing that good lady and her daughter from their slumbers to admit him. The signora and Rosa had not amed many ques- tions of one who paid so liberally. They accepted the story he gave that he was a secret agent of the Italian Government, and that his name was Lancia. They had furnished him with the garb of an Italian workman and hid him. The hue-and-cry died down within a few days. A house of call for Italian

working men is not greaflY concerned in tragedies at millionaires' mansions. The Italian papers of Los Angeles spoke of the murder and the diamond theft, and of the disappearance of the suspected secretary of the murdered man, but the signora and her daughter paid little heed to the story, as to -them it meant neither the sale of one more nor one less bottle of Chianti. That their hidden guest was an agent of the Government was a satisfying thought to them. They rented rooms to those who paid, and further than that concerned themselves but little in the affairs of their patrons. The cunning De Vaux had carefully paved the way to allay all suspicion. So the clamour and search for him passed by the cafe, while he lay in a mean room and chafed at confinement and longed for his dapper attire and fine linen, and drank 'heavily to stifle his fears.

The sentry called for the other guard and fired his rifle to alarm the prison. His comrade joined him, and they were within reach of Luke. whose toes had just touched the ground, when the rope slackened, and with it fell, with a clatter and many heavy thuds, the old prison chimney. It had given way under the bulky weight of the escaring prisoner and fell upon the guards and overwhelmed them. Clambering upon the loose pile of bricks that gave beneath his heavy feet, Like scrambled to the top of the wall, and by some miracle passed over the broken glast and spikes unscathed, and dropped down the sheer twenty feet of the prison wall to liberty.

From a bag on the piano-cart Quabba hastily handed the panting Luke an old coat, trousers, and a hat that had a wig within it. She cried with delight, but the young man counselled silence as someone was approaching. Signora Solari was. in the doorway that looked into the garden. Qualaba was there, and with him was a strange man, quite lame, it would seem, for he leant upon a heavy stick—a mattock handle. "This is my cousin, signora," said Quabba. "He desires a room till he gets a job. Perhaps when he has secured employment you will still honour him by the hospitality of your establishment?" The signora led the new guest to his humble room, gave him .a lamp, and wished him sweet repose. She returned to her daughter and the so charming Signor Lancia of the Italian secret service. The Chianti flowed, caution was forgotten, and the mag- nificent jewel was shown to ravish the eyes of all. _

In the next room a seemingly lame man listened at the thin partition, his eyes bulging, and biting his tongue that he might keep from crying out. For he heard a tipsy voice saying: "You may well admire it. It is called, and rightly, The Diamond from the Sky."

Luke Lovell—for 'it was he—heard the excited conversation from the adjoining room. At last had come an opportunity to repay the kindness of Esther and wipe out in some measure the errors of the past. Softly opening the door of the room in which De Vaux was expatiating upon the wonders of the gem to the two women, Luke crept behind them. The mattock handle descended upon the head of the unfortunate De Vaux. and when the lights were brought The Diamond from the Sky had gone.

div.head: AMONGST THE JUNIORS.
div.p: AMONGST THE JUNIORS.

The leaders of the League paid e, visit to Thelwall-lane last week, inkfull confidence of an easy victory; but in this they received a nasty shock, as the Grappenhall lads turned out to make a strong effort to check the " Saints' " successful march. The opening, portion of the game was very even, and a goal to nil in favour of the " Saints " was a fair criterion of the play. The second portion saw, a more keenly- contested game, as the home team realised the possibility of inflicting defeat on the "Saints," and by adopting open methods they equalised the score. A few 'minutes later they gained the lead, and there were prospects of the "Saints" having to climb down the ladder. It was only a few minutes off time when the scores were made equal again. The remainder of the game was played in semi-darknessl and the visitors very nearly gained the verdict, a fine shot hit- ting the crossbar. When the final whistle was blown the score was two goals each. There was much satisfaction in the home camp at having extracted a point from the leaders. Although Greenhalgh was somewhat easily beaten when the first goal was scored, he made a couple of saves which would have defeated most of the junior goalkeepers.

Rigby was the best full-back Oh the field, and kicked splendidly. W. Jones, a former "Saint," played a fine game against his old colleagues. Rutter is a half-back who will improve as he gains experience.
- Willoughby, although small, get in some good centres.
Povey had not many troublesome shots, but two were put past him.
Tunstall and Furness only gate occasional glimpses of their best form, and had an off-day. Miller was the mainstay of the defence, and also initiated many of the advances of the "Saints."
Owing to a reshuffling of positions, the "Saints'" forwards did not combine .at all satisfactorily. Jones was absent, having a trial at Wilders- pool.

The game in the Park between Rowley and the Recs. proved to be a very keen and exciting struggle. •The majority of the spectators were as excited as the players, favoured the Recs., and spared no efforts in giving vent to their lungs to encourage the players. There were times when robustness in play was -nearly at the extrem. point, and caused the referee plenty of work to keep them under control. At the close of play the result was in favour of the Recs. by two goals against one. There was great rejoicing in the Recs.' camp over the result; they have extracted three points from their rivals in the League fixtures. Rowlinson, Miller, Hassan and Potter were the pick of the United, and for the Recs., Brand- wood was at his best form at full-back. Trainor and Cooper played well in the middle line, and Bate, Gretn and Wilcox were.the pick of the fgrwards.

At Lovely-lane the ground was in a very bad state, and the Cadets and Bewsey Adults played a hard game in the mud. The Cadets held the lead at the interval, but in the second half the Adults equalised after a long bombard- ment of the Cadets' goal. A warm bath would be much appreciated by players after a hard game at Lovely-lane ground.
For to-day's fixtures all the clubs will be en- gaged, and some very interesting games should be witnessed.

St. Elphin's, who, at present, are not ate to put their best team in the field, will have a hard match at Highfield, the latter club having strengthened their ranks quite recently. Howley *United .will appear in the Park, and will have to give of their best to defeat the Trornets.

Probably the keenest game of the day will be at Thelwall-lane, where _Grappenhall and Latchford Recs. will be in opposition. Latchford Cadets will do well if they can bring a point away from Widnes juniors. Penketh and Orford should win on their own grounds.

div.head: "THE RAINY DAY."
div.p: "THE RAINY DAY."

Mr. J. R. Clynes, M.P., in the quarterly report of the National Union of General Workers (Lancashire District) says:— The extension of the unemployment part of the Insurance Act has evoked complaints from a number of workers, who say they ought not to be compelled to pay for a form of insurance which they do not need. Their view is that they will never be out of Work, because they have always been in work. To take this view is to ignore their true interests. To decline to take the benefit of contributions which the State and employers are obliged to pay for the workers' benefit is refusing a gift and for simi- lar refusal other workers have been sorry on previous occasions. Workers have no guarantee of constant work in the future, and those in regular work now can easier afford to pay a small sum for insurance than they can afford to do without benefit when they are un- employed. The skilled trades afford the best examples of provision for the "rainy day." In those trades work has ben most regular, but in those trades at their best the men have seen the wisdom of preparing for the worst of times. In the cotton trade, and other branches of employment, workers who opposed State Un- employment Insurance found themselves when the war brake out totally unable to maintain themselves on account of trade depression. They had then to appeal for State aid, and were glad of the support which previously they had discarded. Men who say it is. hard to pay a few coppers out of low wages will find it harder still to pay for anything when wages are stopped for want of work.

div.head: "OUR DAY" MATINEE.
div.p: "OUR DAY" MATINEE.
Fine Performance And Enthu- siastic Audience.

There was only one verdict upon the mag- nificent Red Cross matinee given last Saturday afternoon—unqualified success; success of the promoters, the artistes, and the management. When Mrs. Henry Greenall went upon the stage and proposed a hearty vote of thanks to all the artistes, the ladies and gentlemen who had got up the programme, and more especially Mr. H. L. Warburton, the manager, who had done the lion's share, one of the largest and most fashionable audiences that ever thronged the Royal Court Theatre signified its enthusiastic approval, and when Miss Sylvia Broadbent, the commandant for Warrington of the Red Cross Society, seconded the proposition, it was carried with vigorous applause. _ _

Pleasure was further shown when the latter lady announced that another performan'ce of "The Twelve Pound Look" would be given at a matinee on December 9th, in aid of the Lord Kitchener Memorial Fund. As already stated, the matinee was a great success, not only from a monetary point of view, but from the excel- lence of the programme arranged for the occasion. The organisers were Mrs. Robert Garnett, Mrs. Fox and Mr. H. L. Warburton, with Mr. Arthur Browne as hon treasurer and Mr. Sidney Wallhead as hon. stage manager. The one-act play called "Love versus Law," was most excellently acted by the Mr. H. Raynor's Repertory Company, who had specially come from Liverpool to help in the matter. The acting was all that could be desired and, in addition to Mr. Raynor, the cast included Mr. John. Blake, Miss Ennis Lawson, Miss Nellie Bonsor and Miss Isa Garnett Vane. The. audience was very much charmed with the dancing of Miss Olga Hughes' little pupils, in a beautiful conception, "The Dance of the Fairies." Miss Mildred Jackson, a wonderfully vivacious child, as a fascinating Pierette, was the life and soul of the performance, while the dancing of Miss Peppy Mathias---a 'tiny tot—was loudly applauded. We had once more the pleasure of hearing some leading members of the Harrison-Frewin Opera Company—Mr. Lewys James, Mr. Furness Williams, Miss Raymonde Amy—who kindly gave their services, coming from St. Helens parposely for the occasion. It was also a great treat to hear Miss Cooke, of the Manchester Concerts, and the fine singing of Mr. A. W. Pearse and Miss Dorothy Goulden. We understand that this was the first appearance of this young lady. She has a

splendid voice, and one capable of great things in the future. Mr. W. H. Payton was accom- panist. The chief attraction of the whole afternoon, however, seemed to be Miss Mona Vivian,. of 'Good Evening" revue, then showing at the Hippodrome, and who appeared by kind per- mission of the management. She first sang "A little broken doll," the chorus of which was joined in by the audience, and had no less than four encores. In response, she gave impersona- tions of George Formby, Yvette Whittaker, and the Dutch-American Girl. Her dancing was also much appreciated. The principal part of the programme was de- voted to an excellent performance of Sir J. M. Barrie's one-act comedy, "The Twelve Pound Look," by some members of the Warrington Dramatic Society. No one was surprised to find that Mrs. Robert. Garnett was selected to play the part of Kate (the typist and Sir Harry Sims first wife) and she simply excelled herself on the occasion. Mr. Sidney Wallhead was the husband, and Mrs. R. W. Budd looked very charming, and played the part of Lady Sims in her Court dress to perfection. It goes without saying that Mr. H. G. Mosley, as the Butler, was, perfect in acting and detail. The stage furniture for the piece was kindly lent by Mr. Ralph Johnsen; and the typewriter by Wood's College, 15, Bridge-street. The theatre orchestra, under Mr: W. C. Pike, musical director, played some capital selections during the afternoon.

div.head: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.
div.p: JOTTINGS BY AN OLD JOURNALIST.

With Experience. At last week's "Lit, and Phil." lecture, Mr. L. Greening confessed that at 20 he thought he knew all about it; at 40 he had his doubts; and at 60 he concluded that he had previously been mistaken. Said an eminent musician: "As a young fellow I said 'I and Mozart'; as I pro- gressed I came to say Mozart and '; now I say 'Mozart.'" I once edited a weekly paper the proprietor of which advertised for a re- porter, and selected from 83 applicants a person of 18 who described himself as a musical and dramatic critic, and made a strong point of his proficiency in French. I sized him up from his letter, and gave the boss my opinion, but he in- sisted on his choice and in due course intro- duced his gem. Said I, • So you are a musician?" "I don't actually play," was the reply. "Anyhow," I continued, "your know- ledge of French will enable me to score a point. M. Poire is giving a series of lectures in French, and of course I shall put you down for that little lot." " Er-well-er," stammered the wretched fraud, "I haven't really done any- thing at it since I left school, but I could rub it up in three months or so, you know." Then I flashed at the discomfited proprietor one of my best, double-barrelled, copper-bottomed, warranted "I -told-you-so "glances, and left him to take his precious bargain away and make the. best of it. Give Credit Where Due.

At the Co-operative Hall meeting on Temper- ance Sunday, the Rev. Irvine Lister implied that bowling greens and billiards are associated with public-houses. No doubt they too Often are, but municipal bovfling greens are steadily increasing everywhere, especially in the indus- trial towns of Lancashire and Yorkshire, as are large halls for billiards purely and simply, for none such that I know of holds a drink licence. As for "rational amusements" being provided for the people out of public funds, so long as 56 years ago Kennington Park, London, lied its well-equipped open-air gymnasium for boys. I then lived with my parents in Manley-place close by, and I well remember how the custodian of the gymnasium, an old soldier and a hater of petticoats, spent most of his time in chasing inquisitive girls from the precincts of the sacred enclosure. That, let me repeat, was at the opening of the 'sixties; nobody would• tolerate such exclusiveness nowadays. However, my point is that Mr. Lister did not take due account of notorious facts. " Livo " Museums.

A Yorkshire observer's flattering reference to the Warrington Museum and Library reminded me of a striking illustration in support of .the claim in last week's paragraph. Thirty or more years ago I lived in a populous industrial dis- trict whose only museum was in the hands of the local Literary and Philosophical Society. It was a port of penny show which nobody ever entered. Eventually the Corporation acquired an estate with a mansion, set up a museum and art gallery, and soon had a large and attractive collection which visitors were free to enter at will without any nonsense about umbrellas and walking sticks. It is so at Rochdale, but at Towneley Hall, Burnley, a penny is charged on each article, even though two or three may be bundled together. At Manchester a courteous attendant gently relieves one of stick or "brolly," but there is no suggestion of baksheesh.

Too Sweet For Anything. No, young man, this is not about "her." It arises upon the Workhouse Master's ingenuous admission that with condensed milk he had con- tinued to use the same quantity of sugar as before, so that inmates liked it because it made the tea sweeter. Many men are fond of over- sweetened tea; I have often noticed it. I once went to a Co-operative Conference, and the local society entertained the delegates at tea, and one who sat opposite to yours truly drank several cups, and into each small cup dropped half-a-dozen good-sized lumps of sugar. That for me constitutes a record, but I have often seen it nearly equalled.

MILN-EVANS.

The marriage of Captain George Gordon Miln, of the Cheshire Regiment, second son of Mr. G. P. Miln, JP., of Chester and Warrington, and Doris, elder daughter of Mr. W. Wynn Evans, solicitor, Wrexham, and Thornycroft, Queen's Park, Chester, took place at St. Mary's Church, Without the Walls, on Monday morning by special licence. The officiating clergymen were the Rev. Canon Grantham and the Rev. R. L. Owen. Owing to Captain Miln's leave from the Front being of short duration, the ceremony was of a very quiet and simple nature, only relatives of the bride and bridegroom's families being invited. The bride and bridegroom left shortly after the ceremony for a short honey- moon, to be spent, at Oxford and 'London. Cap- tain Gordon Miln, who is an M.A. of Oxford, joined the Cheshires as a subaltern soon after the outbreak of war, and has since seen much active service both in Gallipoli and in France, many of his interesting experiences in the first-named theatre of war having been related in our columns. He rejoins his regiment in France again at the end of the present week. Both these families are further represented in His Majesty's Forces at present, Mr. Leslie Wynn Evans, the elder brother of the bride, being an officer in the London Regiment, and a younger brother of the bridegroom, Mr. J. Douglas Miln, like himself, is also an officer in the Cheshires, whilst a third one, Mr. W. Wallace Miln, has recently been transferred from the Royal Fusi- liers to a cadet unit to train for a commission.

The bride's travelling dress was a tailor-made costume and pale blue Chenille hat.

Now is the time to plant roses, theimonth of November being the best month. RoUs like a heavy greasy soil, one that consists of cow or pig manure and old turf chopped up, and if very light, marl or clay should be added. Roses are gross feeders, so plenty of manure should be incorporated with the soil. When planting spread out the roots, and coter up to an inch over the scion or graft, and plant very firm.
